question:
A 58 year old male presents via EMS with worsening shortness of breath for the last 2 days. He reports
worsening leg swelling and needs to sleep on an additional pillow each night. He currently has no chest
pain, but reports a history of a “large” myocardial infarction a few years ago. He does not recall his
medications. Vital signs include a pulse of 100, blood pressure of 170/110, SPO2 of 97% on room air,
and respirations of 14 per minute. Which of the following will provide optimal medical management in
the acute setting? Answer Choices: (A) Administer oral captopril and intravenous furosemide (B)
Administer intravenous nitroglycerin, and intravenous furosemide (C) Administer intravenous
nitroglycerin and oral spironolactone (D) Administer intravenous nitroglycerin, intravenous furosemide,
intravenous metoprolol, and intravenous morphine (E) Administer intravenous nitroglycerin,
intravenous furosemide, and intravenous metoprolol (F) Administer intravenous hydralazine and oral
furosemide (G) Administer intravenous nitroprusside and intravenous furosemide (H) Administer oral
metoprolol and oral furosemide (I) Administer intravenous norepinephrine and intravenous furosemide
(J) Administer oral hydralazine and oral isosorbide dinitrate
 A. Administer intravenous nitroglycerin, intravenous furosemide, and intravenous metoprolol
B. Administer intravenous nitroglycerin and oral spironolactone
C. Administer intravenous hydralazine and oral furosemide
D. Administer oral metoprolol and oral furosemide
E. Administer intravenous nitroglycerin, intravenous furosemide, intravenous metoprolol, and
intravenous morphine
F. Administer oral captopril and intravenous furosemide
G. Administer intravenous nitroprusside and intravenous furosemide
H. Administer oral hydralazine and oral isosorbide dinitrate
I. Administer intravenous nitroglycerin, and intravenous furosemide

J. Administer intravenous norepinephrine and intravenous furosemide
